title: Your bench: real hardware
summary: Test a chip the way engineers do: drive its pins, compare it with the simulation, and track down defects. On screen today, on real boards as they join.

links.why: your finished design goes on the bench to be tested
testing sorts good chips from defective ones
a real chip can disagree with its simulation
links.if: the board and the simulation disagree on one input pattern
links.then: either the chip has a defect or the simulation left something out, and both are worth finding

ideas.how: a defect shows up only on some input patterns, so the test must try them all
the same test runs on a virtual board and a real one: the protocol hides which it is

tradeoffs.how: trying every input pattern finds every single stuck wire, but test time doubles with each extra input

measures.how: each chip that fails the twin test is one that will not ship

then: Chips are tested by large automatic test machines in factories. Nobody outside a chip company can test a chip of their own.
Community shuttles such as Tiny Tapeout (since 2022) send small chips home on demo boards, so anyone can test a design they made.
Browsers can talk to boards over USB (Web Serial in Chrome and Edge, and in Firefox from May 2026), so a web page can be a test bench.

learn.plain: A test bench is like a doctor's check-up for a chip: you give it every input it could see, write down what it answers, and compare with what a healthy chip would say. If one answer is wrong, the pattern of wrong answers points to where the chip is broken.
learn.engineer: A twin test applies every input vector to the device under test and to the reference model and compares the outputs bit by bit. With a single stuck-at fault model, fault diagnosis searches for the faults whose simulated responses match the observed ones on every vector. Real testers add timing (at-speed tests), scan chains for sequential logic and analog measurements, which this bench leaves out.

quiz.q: A 2-bit adder has 4 inputs. How many input patterns does an exhaustive test try?
quiz.why: Each input can be 0 or 1, so 4 inputs give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 patterns.

quiz.q: Two chips fail the same test patterns in the same way. What does that suggest?
options: They probably share the same defect
quiz.why: The wrong answers are a fingerprint: the same fingerprint usually means the same broken wire.

quiz.q: Why does the lab's virtual board speak the same protocol as a real board?
options: So the same test code works on both, and new boards can join without changing it
quiz.why: One small, open protocol lets any board join the bench, and the virtual board keeps that path tested every day.
